milestones.title: the stopwatch
milestones.task: Write measure(fn, args, meter). It calls fn(*args), adds one tick to meter.ticks for every line the candidate executes during the call (including lines of helper functions the candidate defines and calls), restores the previous tracer, and returns fn’s value.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. Hand-counted functions (three statements cost exactly 3 ticks; a helper that is called twice adds its own lines twice; a loop costs the same extra ticks per iteration), meters that accumulate across calls, grader code that costs nothing (even when a candidate calls it), the previous tracer restored after a normal return and after an exception, and ticks spent before an exception still counted. Then the part you came for: the first-draft harness, built on your stopwatch, passes all seven tricks and gives each of them several times the reward of the honest program, and five searches against it all end on a trick.
hints: Two nested functions: local(frame, event, arg) adds a tick when event == "line" and returns itself; global_trace(frame, event, arg) returns local when frame.f_code.co_filename == CANDIDATE and None otherwise.
old = sys.gettrace(), then sys.settrace(global_trace), then try: return fn(*args) finally: sys.settrace(old).

If the grader’s own work is being counted, the filter is missing or wrong. If helper functions of the candidate are not counted, the global function must return local for every candidate frame, not just the first.
If the check complains that tracing is switched off after your function, you restored None where you should restore whatever sys.gettrace() returned before.
milestones.solution:
def measure(fn: Callable, args: tuple, meter: Meter):
    """Call fn(*args) and add one tick to meter.ticks for every line the CANDIDATE executes while it runs.

    Use sys.settrace. The global trace function is called on each new frame ("call" event): return a local
    trace function for frames whose code file is CANDIDATE (frame.f_code.co_filename) and None for every other
    frame, so the grader's own code costs nothing. The local trace function adds a tick on each "line" event
    and returns itself. Return fn's value. Whatever happens, even if fn raises, put back the tracer that was
    installed before (sys.gettrace()) so that measuring never leaves tracing switched on.
    """
    def local(frame, event, arg):
        if event == "line":
            meter.ticks += 1
        return local

    def global_trace(frame, event, arg):
        return local if frame.f_code.co_filename == CANDIDATE else None

    old = sys.gettrace()
    sys.settrace(global_trace)
    try:
        return fn(*args)
    finally:
        sys.settrace(old)
milestones.explain:
Everything else rests on a measurement that is the same on every machine and that the candidate cannot argue with. Wall-clock time is neither: it varies from run to run, depends on the machine, and cannot be checked exactly in a test. Counting executed lines is deterministic, and Python lets you do it from the outside with sys.settrace. You install a trace function; the interpreter calls it with an event name each time something happens. Two events matter here:

  • "call": a new frame (a function, a class body, a module) has just been entered. The global trace function receives it and decides whether to trace that frame: it returns a local trace function to trace it and None to ignore it.
  • "line": the frame is about to execute a new line. The local trace function receives it. Add one tick and return the local trace function again, so that the next line is traced too.

The part that makes this a stopwatch for candidates and not for everything is the filter. Candidate code is compiled under the file name "<candidate>" (the constant CANDIDATE), so a frame belongs to the candidate exactly when frame.f_code.co_filename == CANDIDATE. The grader’s own lines, the builtins that run inside sorted, the check itself, must cost nothing. And the stopwatch must put things back: if something else was tracing (a debugger, a coverage tool), measure has to restore that tracer when it finishes, even when the candidate raises.
milestones.card:
A harness that rewards speed needs a clock that reads the same on every machine and that the candidate (the program being scored) cannot argue with. Counting executed lines is such a clock: one tick per line. Python lets you watch a program from outside. sys.settrace(f) makes the interpreter call f on events, a "call" event when a function starts and a "line" event before each line runs.

measure(fn, args, meter) needs two functions. The global trace function receives each "call" and returns a local trace function to follow that frame's lines, or None to ignore the frame. Follow only frames whose frame.f_code.co_filename is CANDIDATE, so the grader's own lines cost nothing. The local one adds a tick to meter.ticks on each "line" and returns itself. Save sys.gettrace() first and restore it in a finally, even if the candidate raises. Return what fn returns.

A body of three statements costs exactly 3 ticks; a helper it calls twice adds its own lines twice.

Read more: A0 chapter 21, budgets: stopping a program that never ends.

milestones.title: a check the output cannot fool
milestones.task: Write strict_equal(out, want): true only if out is exactly a Python int equal to want.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. Exact ints (including 0, negatives and huge numbers) pass; different numbers fail; and nine impostors are rejected: an object whose __eq__ always returns True, an int subclass with a lying __eq__, True against 1, False against 0, the float 5.0, the string "5", None, a list and a tuple. Then at the harness level: the always-equal trick passes everything and earns 65.8 under out == want, passes nothing and earns 0 under strict_equal, and the honest program’s reward is identical under both.
hints: One line: return type(out) is int and out == want. The and short-circuits, so == only runs once the type is known to be exactly int.
If the check says an int subclass was accepted, you used isinstance. If it says True was accepted against 1, you compared first or used isinstance (a bool is an int).
milestones.solution:
def strict_equal(out, want) -> bool:
    """True only if `out` is exactly a Python int (type(out) is int: not a bool, not a subclass, not a float,
    not an object that defines __eq__) and out == want."""
    return type(out) is int and out == want
milestones.explain:
The first door is the shortest. The first-draft check is out == want, and Python evaluates that by asking the left-hand object whether it equals the right-hand one. The always-equal trick returns an instance of a class whose __eq__ answers True to everything, so the check passes eight tests that were never answered. The candidate chose the object whose code decides the comparison, which is to say it graded itself.

The repair is to compare only things the grader can trust, and to do the type test before any comparison that could run the candidate’s code. The right type is exactly int: not bool (True == 1), not an int subclass that overrides __eq__, not 5.0, not "5". The test is type(out) is int, and not isinstance(out, int), because isinstance accepts the subclass that lies. This is a tiny example of the first control in chapter 15, “check the thing, not a symptom”: a check that asks only whether something compares equal is a check of the candidate’s cooperation.
milestones.card:
The check out == want lets the candidate answer for itself. Python asks the left-hand object, the candidate's output, whether it equals the right-hand one, and an object whose __eq__ always returns True agrees to everything. The repair is to compare only things the grader can trust, and to test the type before any comparison that could run the candidate's code.

strict_equal(out, want) is true only if out is exactly an int and equals want. Use type(out) is int, not isinstance(out, int): isinstance also accepts an int subclass whose __eq__ lies, and bool is such a subclass (True == 1). Put the type test first, so the == never runs on a stranger.

strict_equal(5, 5)     -> True
strict_equal(True, 1)  -> False
strict_equal(5.0, 5)   -> False

milestones.title: a world that holds nothing of the grader’s
milestones.task: Write run_isolated(source, xs, k): load the candidate in a new namespace with a throwaway Meter and no extras, call solve(tuple(xs), k) and return what it returns. Let any exception the candidate raises, at load time or in solve, propagate.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. Honest programs return the right ints, on an empty list and with repeats; the candidate receives a tuple; programs that touch FS or CLOCK fail with NameError (nothing of the grader’s exists there); a counter the candidate keeps in a global is 1 on every call, never 2 (a new world each time); a candidate’s ValueError, an import (there is no __import__) and a syntax error all propagate. At the harness level, with strict=True already on, peek and tamper written without a fallback earn 65.8 and 32.9 on a shared disk and 0 when isolated, and an honest program keeps its reward.
hints: Two lines: ns = load_world(source, Meter()) then return ns["solve"](tuple(xs), k). The point is what you do not pass: no extras argument at all.
If the check says a counter reached 2, you reused a namespace between calls (for instance by caching the loaded world).
Do not wrap the call in try/except: whether a crash scores zero or is retried is the harness’s decision, not the runner’s.
milestones.solution:
def run_isolated(source: str, xs, k):
    """Run the candidate on ONE test and return what solve returned, letting any exception it raises (at load
    time or in solve) propagate.

    The candidate gets a brand-new namespace for this call alone, built with load_world and a throwaway Meter,
    and NO extras: it cannot see the grader's disk, clock or answer key, and nothing it stored in a previous
    call exists. It is handed a tuple copy of the input.
    """
    ns = load_world(source, Meter())
    return ns["solve"](tuple(xs), k)
milestones.explain:
The next door is not about the output. It is about what the candidate can see. In the first draft the candidate runs in a namespace that also holds FS, the dictionary standing in for a shared disk, and CLOCK. Two tricks use the disk. peek looks up the answer to its own input in the key and returns it. tamper goes further and writes its own answer over the key, because the checker reads the key back after the run and will be comparing the candidate’s answer with the candidate’s answer. This is the “reward that reads its own output file” family of chapter 15, with METR’s runs that read the reference answer from the call stack and patched the evaluator as its real-world form: the grader and the candidate share state, so the candidate can edit the thing that judges it.

The defence is the standard one in security (threat modelling): a small trusted core and a narrow channel. The candidate gets a fresh world for every call, built with load_world and no extras: no disk, no clock, no key, nothing that a previous call left behind. It is handed a tuple copy of its input, so it cannot change what the grader holds. What comes back across the boundary is one value, the return value. In this lab the boundary is a new namespace; in a real harness it is a process or a container with no access to the grader’s files (Sandboxes & Permissions).
milestones.card:
What a candidate can see matters as much as what it returns. If it runs in the same namespace as the grader's disk and clock, it can read the answer key from that disk, or overwrite the key with its own answer before the grader reads it back. The standard defence is a small trusted core and a narrow channel: each call gets a fresh world that holds nothing of the grader's, and only the return value crosses back.

run_isolated(source, xs, k) builds that world with load_world (already written), a throwaway Meter and no extras. It then calls solve in it on tuple(xs) and k. The tuple copy means the candidate cannot change the grader's list. Return what solve returns and let exceptions propagate: the harness decides that a crash earns nothing. Because the world is rebuilt for every call, nothing a candidate stored in a global survives to the next one.

a candidate that counts its calls in a global returns 1 every time
a candidate that reads FS fails with NameError

Read more: A7 chapter 15, hardening an evaluator.

milestones.title: a clock the candidate cannot reach
milestones.task: Write cold_ticks(source, xs, k), returning the ticks of loading the candidate in a fresh world with a private meter and calling solve(tuple(xs), k) once. Exceptions propagate.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. Hand counts (a one-line def plus a one-line return is exactly 2 ticks; two load lines and two call lines is 4); deterministic and at least n for sorting n numbers; the selection loop costs more than twice the sorted one-liner; a 50-iteration loop at import time costs 100 ticks or more; the memoising program costs the same each time and at least what its plain version costs; the rewind trick finds no clock and costs at least the honest work; a program that writes to CLOCK fails with NameError. At the harness level, with strict and isolated already on, peek, tamper, memo, rewind and the padded peek each gain more than 1.5 reward points over the honest program before cold timing and less than 0.25 after; the honest program keeps a reward above 1.5; and the lookup trick is still open.
hints: Three lines: meter = Meter(); ns = load_world(source, meter); measure(ns["solve"], (tuple(xs), k), meter); then return meter.ticks.
If the check says the 2-tick program cost 1, the load went onto a different meter than the call. Use one meter for both.
If memo still pays, you are probably calling a loaded world twice; each call of cold_ticks must build its own.
milestones.solution:
def cold_ticks(source: str, xs, k) -> int:
    """The ticks one test costs, measured by the grader: a fresh world for this call (load_world with a Meter
    that only the grader holds and NO extras), the load counted, then one call of solve(tuple(xs), k) measured
    on the same meter. Returns meter.ticks. Exceptions from the candidate propagate."""
    meter = Meter()
    ns = load_world(source, meter)
    measure(ns["solve"], (tuple(xs), k), meter)
    return meter.ticks
milestones.explain:
The timer has three problems at once, and each is a real habit. It runs every test three times in one warm namespace and keeps the fastest (“to remove noise”), so a program that remembers its answers, memo, pays full price once and almost nothing twice. It starts the clock after the program has loaded, so any work done at import time is free. And the meter itself, CLOCK, is a name in the candidate’s world, so rewind can read it before the work and write the old value back after. The first two are the ordinary mistakes of benchmarking: warm-ups, caches and best-of-N change what is being measured, which is why benchmark tools such as hyperfine make them explicit choices. The third is chapter 15’s “overwrote the timer the grader uses.”

One principle fixes all three: the grader owns the meter, and every measurement starts cold. cold_ticks builds a new world for one test with a Meter that only the grader holds, loads the candidate under measurement (so setup work counts, because load_world already runs the load through your stopwatch), then calls solve once on the same meter and returns the total. No repeats, no warm cache, no reachable clock. Total cost for the candidate is its load plus its call, for every test, as a user starting a fresh process would see it.
milestones.card:
The leaky timer has three flaws. It runs each test three times in one warm namespace and keeps the fastest, so a program that remembers its answers (memoisation) pays once and is nearly free after. It starts the clock after loading, so work done at import time costs nothing. And the meter is a name the candidate can reach, so it can read the clock before the work and write the old value back after. One principle fixes all three: the grader owns the meter, and every measurement starts cold.

cold_ticks(source, xs, k) makes a Meter that only the grader holds, builds a new world with load_world and no extras (it already counts the load, through measure), then measures one call of solve on tuple(xs) and k against the same meter. No repeats, no reused namespace. Return meter.ticks: the load plus the call, as a fresh process would see it. Exceptions propagate.

def solve(xs, k):   # 1 tick when loaded
    return 0        # 1 tick when called: 2 in all

Read more: A7 chapter 15, hardening an evaluator.

milestones.title: fresh, awkward inputs
milestones.task: Write hidden_tests(seed, n), returning n tests (xs, k) with the shape above.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. For five seeds: ten tests with 0 <= k <= len(xs) and integer values; tests 0 to 3 are exactly the four special cases; the random tests respect the size and value ranges; no test equals a visible one; the same seed gives the same tests even if the global generator is reseeded in between; another seed gives other tests; k takes many values over 60 seeds, including 0; and the first n tests are a prefix of a longer list. At the harness level: against fixed tests the lookup trick gains 9.1 reward points over the honest program (with cold, isolated, strict harness already on) and against fresh ones −0.2; the sorted(xs)[-k:] program passes all eight visible tests with a healthy reward and earns exactly 0 on the hidden ones; and the honest program varies a little across rounds but stays above 1.5.
hints: rng = random.Random(seed) and a loop while len(tests) < n that builds test number len(tests) by if/elif on the index.
A helper draw(size, lo=-50, hi=99) returning [rng.randint(lo, hi) for _ in range(size)] keeps the cases short.
Redraw only if (tuple(xs), k) is in the set of visible tests; the special cases 2 and 3 cannot collide, but one rule for all is simpler.
If the check says the first n tests are not a prefix, you are consuming random numbers in an order that depends on n.
milestones.solution:
def hidden_tests(seed: int, n: int) -> List[Tuple[List[int], int]]:
    """n tests (xs, k) with 0 <= k <= len(xs), reproducible from `seed` and independent of the global random state
    (use rng = random.Random(seed)). The first tests are fixed in kind, the rest are random:

        0   a list of 5 to 10 numbers with k = 0                 (the case sorted(xs)[-k:] gets wrong)
        1   a list of 5 to 10 numbers with k = len(xs)           (take everything)
        2   a list of 8 to 12 numbers drawn from -2..2, so full of repeats, with 1 <= k < len(xs)
        3   the empty list with k = 0
        4+  len(xs) uniform in 1..16, numbers uniform in -50..99, k uniform in 0..len(xs)

    Random lists use numbers from -50 to 99 (negatives included) unless said otherwise. Test 0, 1 and 4+ should
    not be a visible test (reject and redraw if one comes up).
    """
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    seen = {(tuple(xs), k) for xs, k in VISIBLE}

    def draw(size, lo=-50, hi=99):
        return [rng.randint(lo, hi) for _ in range(size)]

    tests = []
    while len(tests) < n:
        i = len(tests)
        if i == 0:
            xs = draw(rng.randint(5, 10)); k = 0
        elif i == 1:
            xs = draw(rng.randint(5, 10)); k = len(xs)
        elif i == 2:
            xs = draw(rng.randint(8, 12), -2, 2); k = rng.randint(1, len(xs) - 1)
        elif i == 3:
            xs, k = [], 0
        else:
            xs = draw(rng.randint(1, 16)); k = rng.randint(0, len(xs))
        if (tuple(xs), k) in seen:
            continue
        tests.append((xs, k))
    return tests
milestones.explain:
The lookup trick answers the eight visible tests from a table and solves everything else honestly. Against eight fixed tests it is the best program there is: three ticks a test instead of thirty. It is also, strictly, a legitimate answer to the question the harness asked, which is the lesson. The harness asked about eight inputs, so the search optimised for eight inputs. This is the answer-key family of chapter 15 (“recognising test inputs”), and the cure is the one Ofria found when he randomised the test: generate the tests inside the grader, from a seed the candidate never sees, and change them.

Fresh tests also fix a second problem that has nothing to do with cheating. Look again at the honest-looking third algorithm, sorted(xs)[-k:]. It passes every visible test, because every visible test has k of at least 1. Its bug only shows when k is 0, and nobody wrote that test. A hidden-test generator is a way of writing the tests you forgot, so it should not be uniform noise: it should put the awkward cases first. Yours produces, for any seed, the same list of tests:

  • Test 0: a list of 5 to 10 numbers with k = 0. This is the case that sinks sorted(xs)[-k:].
  • Test 1: a list of 5 to 10 numbers with k equal to the length: take everything.
  • Test 2: 8 to 12 numbers from −2 to 2, so full of repeats, with 1 ≤ k < length.
  • Test 3: the empty list with k = 0.
  • Tests 4 onwards: 1 to 16 numbers from −50 to 99 and a random k from 0 to the length. Redraw any test that coincides with a visible one.

Two details are about reproducibility. Use your own random.Random(seed), never the global generator, so that the same seed always gives the same tests and a test elsewhere in the program cannot change them. And note how the harness uses it: evaluate(source, round) draws the tests for that round, and the search compares the current program and its variation on the same round, then moves to a new round on the next step. Fresh tests on every step stop the search memorising them; a shared draw within a step stops the comparison being dominated by which list sizes happened to come up (the paired comparison of Statistics for Evals).
milestones.card:
If the same eight tests are used on every evaluation, a search learns them: a lookup table of their answers beats every honest program. The cure is to generate tests inside the grader from a seed the candidate never sees, and to change them. A generator also writes the tests you forgot, so it puts the awkward cases first.

hidden_tests(seed, n) returns n pairs (xs, k) with 0 <= k <= len(xs). Draw everything in order from your own random.Random(seed), never the global generator, so a seed always gives the same tests and the first n tests are a prefix of any longer list. The docstring fixes the first four tests (k = 0, k = len(xs), many repeats, the empty list) and the ranges of the random ones. Redraw a test that equals one in VISIBLE.

xs = [3, 1, 2], k = 0: the answer is 0
sum(sorted(xs)[-k:]) gives 6, because [-0:] is the whole list

Read more: A7 chapter 15, hardening an evaluator.

milestones.title: results that are too good to be true
milestones.task: Write tripwire(total_ticks, tests): true if total_ticks is below the sum of len(xs) over the tests with k >= 1.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. Hand cases (over lists of 3, 2 and 4 numbers with k = 1, 0, 2 the bound is 7: 6 ticks is flagged, 7 and 8 are not; with every k equal to 0 nothing is ever flagged; reading one number at one tick is exactly at the bound and passes); the honest loop and the honest sorted program are never flagged on 40 draws of hidden tests; with only the tripwire on, the six cheap tricks are flagged and earn 0 while the padded peek is not flagged and still earns more than 1.5 times the honest program. Then the whole hardened harness (strict, isolated, cold, hidden and guard): no trick gains 0.3 reward points over the honest program; the honest program earns more than 1.8 and is not flagged; the sorted(xs)[-k:] bug earns 0; and eight searches all end on sorted with a harness score within 35% of the audit’s.
hints: return total_ticks < sum(len(xs) for xs, k in tests if k >= 1).
If an honest program is flagged, check the comparison is strict (<, not <=) and that you excluded only the k = 0 tests, not short lists.
milestones.solution:
def tripwire(total_ticks: int, tests) -> bool:
    """True if a passing candidate used suspiciously few ticks. To get the top k of a list a program must look at
    every number at least once, and looking costs at least one tick each, so over a set of tests any honest
    candidate needs at least the SUM of len(xs) over the tests with k >= 1. Flag total_ticks below that bound."""
    return total_ticks < sum(len(xs) for xs, k in tests if k >= 1)
milestones.explain:
The five defences above each close a door someone has already walked through. The last control in this lab is for doors nobody has seen yet. Chapter 15 lists it as “add anomaly tripwires”: some results are too good to be true, and a rule can say so without understanding the trick. METR’s method for RE-Bench was of this kind, review the anomalously high-scoring runs first.

A good tripwire comes from a bound that no honest candidate can beat. Here there is a clean one. To return the sum of the k largest numbers of a list, any program must look at every number at least once, because a number it never looked at could be the largest. In this meter looking costs at least one tick per number. So over a set of tests, any honest candidate needs at least the sum of len(xs) over the tests with k at least 1 (a test with k = 0 needs no reading: the answer is 0). A candidate that passes every test in fewer ticks than that has not computed the answer; it has found a shortcut. tripwire(total_ticks, tests) flags it, and the harness scores a flagged candidate zero.

The chart shows the tripwire working and shows its limit. On ten hidden tests the honest programs use 322 (sorted) and 800 (loop) ticks against a bound of 57. Five tricks finish at 10 to 30 ticks, far below the bound, and are flagged. The sixth, peek_padded, does the same peek but first copies the list, pad = list(xs), which costs exactly the length of the list in ticks; it lands at 95, above the bound, and the tripwire does not flag it. It still beats the honest program by a wide margin. A tripwire detects an exploit that is greedy; it does not remove the loophole, and a searching process that is penalised for being greedy tends to learn to be only as greedy as it can afford (Baker et al. report the same when a monitor is trained against, chapter 15). So the tripwire is the last milestone and the last layer: it catches what the other five missed or what someone adds to the menu tomorrow, and it flags the programs a human should read.
milestones.card:
Some results are too good to be true, and a rule can say so without understanding the trick. A good tripwire comes from a bound that no honest candidate can beat. To return the sum of the k largest numbers, a program must read every number at least once, because one it skipped could be the largest, and here reading costs at least one tick per number. Passing in fewer ticks than that means a shortcut.

tripwire(total_ticks, tests) takes the ticks summed over all tests and the list of (xs, k) pairs. The bound is the sum of len(xs) over the tests with k >= 1: with k = 0 the answer is 0 and nothing needs reading. Return True only if total_ticks is below the bound (exactly at it is fine). The harness then scores a flagged candidate zero. A tripwire is a net, not a wall: a cheat that burns a few spare ticks to stay above the bound gets through.

lists of 5 and 8 numbers, k = 3 and 0: bound = 5
4 ticks is flagged; 5 ticks is not
